verdict.reasoning: The only positive observations are two total absences at the entry service: zero traces [tr_77d8e6acee83] and zero log lines [tr_b42ca415bd08]. The trace specialist noted the absence is total, not partial, which is inconsistent with a sampled, partially-degraded path. Metric emptiness carries no weight either way — all three metric dispatches failed as unavailable span-metric series, and the same gap exists in the pre-incident baseline, making it a standing instrumentation condition [tr_e44cb5f7f0bc][tr_28928cb4f5ae]. The change log rules out update, repoint, human edit, and redeploy on nginx, leaving only first-creation records and a quiet six-minute gap before onset [tr_71f8714f5626]. Among the hang-alike classes, a network_partition would normally leave the service's own log complaining it cannot reach upstreams, and disk_fill or bad_config would usually emit a diagnostic line; nginx wrote nothing at all. compose-post-service's silence [tr_bdff52fbd51f] follows from a frozen front door forwarding nothing, so no second fault is required.
verdict.root_cause: The front-door service nginx-web-server stopped doing work while remaining reachable: across the full ~30-minute window spanning onset it emitted no access or error log lines [tr_b42ca415bd08] and not a single span [tr_77d8e6acee83], which is anomalous for an edge proxy that normally logs every request. No change landed between its creation burst and onset to explain a content-level regression [tr_71f8714f5626], and downstream compose-post-service is equally silent [tr_bdff52fbd51f] because nothing is being forwarded to it. Total silence from the alerting entry service with no error signal anywhere is the signature of a stopped process whose socket still accepts, leaving callers to hang to their deadlines. Confidence is low: every metric dispatch returned an unavailable series rather than a measurement [tr_28928cb4f5ae][tr_e44cb5f7f0bc][tr_5c01829f25f9], and both log queries used pod-name regexes that could themselves have missed the pods.

alternatives.why_not: The change record shows a first creation with no prior version to regress from and no failed-create, restart, or retry entries [tr_71f8714f5626]; onset followed a quiet six-minute gap rather than coinciding with creation. Viable only because pod status was never read.
alternatives.root_cause: The nginx-thrift workload created six minutes before onset never started correctly, so the edge never served or logged anything.

alternatives.why_not: Zero spans and zero log lines exist for the entry service itself [tr_77d8e6acee83][tr_b42ca415bd08]; a proxy blocked on a slow backend would still log requests and timeouts. Nothing in the evidence implicates compose-post-service specifically [tr_ab2c2dafb187].
alternatives.root_cause: compose-post-service stalled and nginx merely hung waiting on it, making the edge the service that noticed rather than the culprit.

open_questions: Pod status and restart counts were never retrieved for nginx-thrift or compose-post-service; a crash-loop or never-ready pod looks identical to a freeze from these dispatches.

Both Loki queries used pod-name regexes rather than a namespace label and returned an inconsistent truncation flag [tr_b42ca415bd08][tr_bdff52fbd51f], so the zero-match may be a selector miss rather than genuine silence.
No caller-side evidence was gathered: whether clients hang to deadline or receive immediate errors is the distinction the verdict turns on, and it is unestablished.

sections.body:
The page came from nginx-web-server, the edge proxy and entry point for the social-network stack. Blast radius as scoped on arrival was four services, severity critical. The first instinct on an edge-proxy page is to look for a 5xx burst and name the upstream that caused it, so that is where the first dispatches went.

The immediate surprise was that there was nothing to look at. A trace query scoped to nginx-web-server across the full ~30-minute window spanning onset returned not one span. Not a degraded subset, not slow spans — zero. For a front door that normally carries continuous traffic, an empty trace result is itself the finding, and it closed off the plan of attributing the problem to a specific downstream call. Nothing could be implicated and nothing could be exonerated on trace evidence.
sections.heading: What the alert said and what we saw first

sections.body:
Around T+3m the log query came back the same way: a Loki query for the nginx frontend pods in the social-network namespace returned zero lines over the whole window. No access lines, no error lines, so no upstream names and no upstream status codes. Routine access logging alone should have produced thousands of lines; its total absence is not compatible with a healthy, serving, well-logged proxy.

Two caveats a future responder should carry forward. First, the selector matched on a pod-name regex rather than a namespace-wide or label-based selector, so a zero match is equally consistent with a selector miss. Second, the result came back carrying a truncation flag while also being empty, which is internally inconsistent and should lower trust in it further. The honest reading is: nginx-web-server is probably silent, but this query cannot distinguish silent from unqueried.
sections.heading: The log path, and why it only half-counts

sections.body:
Three separate metric dispatches were spent chasing error ratios — on nginx-web-server, on compose-post-service, and on home-timeline-service. All three came back empty, and all three were empty for the same structural reason: the error-ratio template reads span-derived metrics, and this Prometheus holds none for these services because they do not emit traces that get converted into metrics.

This is the trap worth flagging. The empty result is *unavailable*, not *measured zero*. It does not mean the services were error-free, it does not mean they were idle, and it does not mean traffic stopped. Crucially, the same absence is present in the pre-onset baseline window, so it predates the incident entirely and is a standing instrumentation condition rather than a symptom. Retrying or widening the time range on these templates will not help; the data was never stored. Status-code breakdowns and upstream latency profiles ride on the same missing pipeline, so neither can be recovered from this source — they would have to come from access logs or an nginx exporter.
sections.heading: Dead end: the metrics dispatches

sections.body:
Both change-log pulls looked promising and both turned out not to matter. For nginx-web-server, the only records in the 24-hour window were three creation events from the platform-automation actor roughly six minutes before onset: a ConfigMap, a Service, and the workload container, created within moments of each other. There were no updates, no patches, no redeploys, no routing flips — and, importantly, a quiet gap of about six minutes between the creation burst and onset with no activity at all. There is no last-minute edit to blame.

One nuance that cuts the other way: because the container record is a *first* creation rather than a replacement, there was no established steady state. A configuration wrong from first boot stays on the table even though a regression-against-a-previous-version does not.

compose-post-service told the same story: three changes, all at one moment roughly six minutes before onset, all from platform-automation, workload created fresh. No failure, rollback, restart or retry entries appear, so the change log does not show compose-post-service failing to come up — but neither does it confirm that it did. The change-log scope was per-service, so whether peer backends came up in the same burst was never established.
sections.heading: Dead end: the change histories

sections.body:
The last dispatch went to compose-post-service's logs on the theory that a downstream crash or connection failure would explain the edge going dark. It returned nothing: no lines of any level across the full window. No crash, no panic, no connection-failure message pointing at a database or cache, and no repeated startup sequences that would betray a restart loop.

The same selector caveat applies — pod-name regex, inconsistent truncation flag — so this empty result is provisional too. But read alongside the nginx silence it fits a simple shape: nothing is being forwarded to compose-post-service, so compose-post-service has nothing to say.
sections.heading: Following the silence downstream

sections.body:
The picture we converged on: nginx-web-server stopped doing work while remaining reachable. No logs, no spans, no error signal anywhere, no change landing between its creation and onset to explain a content-level regression, and a downstream that is equally quiet because nothing is reaching it. Total silence from the alerting entry service, with no errors recorded on any path, is the signature of a stopped process whose socket still accepts connections — callers hang until their deadlines rather than getting a refusal they could log.

Fix class: restart.

Confidence in this is low, and that should be stated plainly rather than softened. Every metric dispatch returned an unavailable series rather than a measurement, and both log queries used selectors that could have missed their targets on their own.
sections.heading: Where the investigation landed

sections.body:
Three things were never checked, and any one of them could overturn the conclusion.

Pod status and restart counts were never retrieved for the nginx frontend pods or for compose-post-service. From the dispatches we ran, a crash-loop or a never-ready pod is indistinguishable from a stopped-but-listening process. This is the cheapest gap to close and should be the first move next time.

Both log queries used pod-name regexes rather than a namespace label, and both returned an inconsistent truncation flag alongside an empty body. Re-query with a broader selector before treating the silence as real.

No caller-side evidence was gathered at all. Whether clients hang to their deadline or get an immediate connection error is precisely the distinction this conclusion rests on, and it was never established. If callers are seeing prompt refusals, the stopped-process reading is wrong and the investigation should restart from scheduling and readiness.
sections.heading: Open questions for whoever reads this next

proposal.risk: The risk of abstaining is prolonged outage: if the diagnosis is right, the front door stays silent until someone acts. The risk I am declining to take is larger in expectation — restart_service is marked irreversible, it discards in-process state, and on a service created only six minutes before onset [tr_71f8714f5626] a recreate would destroy the one instance whose pod status nobody has yet read. If the real mechanism is a never-ready pod, a bad image pull, or a misconfiguration present from first boot (explicitly left viable by the change-history analysis), the restart reproduces the same broken state and burns the diagnostic evidence that would have identified it, while the recreate itself looks like remediation and may be mistaken for one.
proposal.if_wrong: This abstention is wrong if the service is genuinely frozen and every minute of delay is lost availability at the front door. The observation that would overturn it is narrow and cheap: pod phase Running with restartCount stable at its creation value for nginx-thrift, plus a namespace-scoped Loki query that still returns zero lines for that pod while returning lines for its peers. That combination would meet the restart precondition and I would propose restart_service on nginx-web-server immediately. Conversely, a climbing restartCount, a Pending/CrashLoopBackOff phase, or logs appearing under a broader selector would each confirm the abstention and redirect the investigation.
proposal.blast_radius: Had the restart been proposed, it would hit nginx-web-server alone for the duration of the container recreate, and its callers would see connection resets — in this incident's graph that is every external client of the front door, plus the three downstreams it fans out to (compose-post-service, home-timeline-service, user-timeline-service), which would see traffic cut and then resume. As an abstention, the blast radius is informational only: the on-call reader is told the incident is unremediated and is handed two specific queries to run before anyone acts.
proposal.expected_effect: No action proposed, so no effect is predicted. The only legal candidate was restart_service on nginx-web-server, and its precondition — 'the evidence points at process state rather than at a change' — is not met. Every dispatch behind the freeze diagnosis is an absence, not a measurement: the error-ratio series was reported unavailable rather than zero for nginx-web-server [tr_28928cb4f5ae], the trace query returned no spans at all [tr_77d8e6acee83], and both log queries used pod-name regexes (nginx-thrift-*, compose-post-service-*) rather than a namespace/app label and returned an inconsistent truncation flag alongside their zero matches [tr_b42ca415bd08][tr_bdff52fbd51f]. No pod status, phase, or restart count was ever retrieved for either service, so a frozen process, a never-ready pod, a crash-loop, and a selector miss in Loki are all equally consistent with what is on the board. Change history shows only a first creation six minutes before onset with no mutation after [tr_71f8714f5626], which rules out rollback_image and revert_config (no prior image or config exists to return to) but does not positively establish process state either. Before any action: fetch pod phase and restartCount for nginx-thrift and compose-post-service, and re-run Loki with a namespace-only selector ({namespace="social-network"}) to distinguish genuine silence from a selector miss. If restartCount is climbing, the fix class is not restart; if the pod is Running with zero restarts and the namespace-wide log query is still empty for these pods, restart_service becomes well-founded.
